nodeData.note: Edexcel International GCSE Physics, Paper 1, code 4 P H 1 slash 1 P. Two hours, 110 marks, about 61 percent of the grade. You may use a calculator. Paper 1 covers the core content only, not the extra Paper 2 content. Each branch is one question type: read the question, find the key words, plan, write, check. Then five spoken questions. Draft: needs review by a physics teacher. (Source: spec pages 8 and 29.)

children.note: These questions ask you to recall a fact, a word, or a definition. Multiple choice questions also start with what, why or which. They are usually worth one mark and test knowledge, assessment objective 1. Spend about one minute. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 7 to 9.)
Listen for the command word. State, give and name all mean the same: recall the fact. No reason is needed. (Source: spec page 47.)
Mark the exact thing asked for, and how many. If it says tick one box, tick only one. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 7.)
No plan needed. Think of the exact physics word, not a word that sounds close to it. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 8.)
Write the word or the definition, short and exact. Use the definition you learned word for word. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 89.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
A related but wrong word, for example gravitational field strength instead of gravity. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 8.
Ticking more than one box in a row, or more boxes than asked. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 7, and Paper 2 report page 11.
Explaining, or adding extra wrong items, when you only had to name. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 12.
A definition not learned exactly, for example voltage as current times resistance. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 89.
Repeating the words of the question, which earns nothing. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 24.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: Do state, give and name mean different things? Answer: No. They all mean recall the fact. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 7 to 9.)
Ask: Do you need a reason for a state question? Answer: No. Just the fact. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 7 to 9.)
Ask: If the question says tick one box, how many do you tick? Answer: Only one. Two ticks lose the mark. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 7 to 9.)
Ask: What is voltage? Answer: The energy transferred per unit charge passed. A volt is a joule per coulomb. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 7 to 9.)
Ask: About how long for a one mark question? Answer: About one minute. That is our suggestion. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 7 to 9.)

Describe means give an account of something. Your statements should be linked, but you do not need to give a reason. These questions are often two or three marks and test knowledge, assessment objective 1. Spend about two or three minutes. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 10.)
Listen for describe. You say what happens, in order. You do not need to say why. (Source: spec page 47.)
Mark the thing to describe and any table or graph you must use. Answers about the data given score best. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 10.)
Count the marks. Plan one clear point for each mark, in a sensible order. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 107.)
Write short linked sentences. Use the correct physics words and quote numbers from the data where you can. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 10.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
A general answer that does not use the table given. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 10.
Describing the wrong property, for example size instead of mass compared with the Sun. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 13.
Answering a nearby question instead of the one asked. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 4.
Vague words, for example electrons removed from objects, instead of from atoms. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 23.
Mixing up energy stores and energy transfers. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 16.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: Does describe need a reason? Answer: No. Say what happens. A reason is for explain. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 10.)
Ask: How many points for a three mark describe? Answer: At least three clear points. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 10.)
Ask: If the question gives a table, what must you use? Answer: The data in that table. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 10.)
Ask: A star is blue. What does that tell you? Answer: It is very hot. Blue stars are hotter than red stars. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 10.)
Ask: Name two energy transfers. Answer: Any two of: mechanically, electrically, by heating, by radiation. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 10.)

Explain means give a point and a reason. The reason can be a physics idea or a calculation. These questions are often two to four marks and test knowledge and applying it, assessment objectives 1 and 2. Spend about two to four minutes. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 6 and 19.)
Listen for explain. Every point needs a because. (Source: spec page 47.)
Mark what changes and which way. Many students got the change the wrong way round. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 19.)
Make a chain: this changes, so that changes, so this happens. Pick one line of argument and keep to it. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 46.)
Write each link of the chain as a sentence. Start with the equation if one fits, and use it to explain. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 46.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Saying what changes but not why. June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 6 and 19.
Getting the change backwards, for example thermistor resistance going up instead of down. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 19.
Mixing two different arguments in one answer. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 46.
Mixing up wavefronts, wavelength and waves. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 62.
Vague words like dangerous, instead of the exact harm. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 77.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What must every explain point have? Answer: A reason. A because. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 6 and 19.)
Ask: A thermistor gets hotter. What happens to its resistance? Answer: It goes down. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 6 and 19.)
Ask: Why does a moving puck on ice slow down? Answer: Friction acts in the opposite direction to its velocity. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 6 and 19.)

Ask: Pressure in water: why is it bigger deeper down? Answer: There is a greater height of water above, and pressure difference equals height times density times g. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 6 and 19.)

Ask: Should you write the word dangerous? Answer: No. Say the exact harm, for example it damages cells or causes cancer. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 6 and 19.)

Calculate means get a number and show your working. Show that and determine questions work the same way. These questions are often two to four marks and test applying physics, assessment objective 2. The spec says you must learn eighteen Paper 1 equations by heart; open the Plan bubble to hear them. Spend about one minute per mark. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 47, command words, and pages 51 to 52, equations to recall.)
Listen for the number of marks and for the unit you must give. A show that question gives you the answer to check. (Source: spec page 48.)
Underline each value with its unit. Change centimetres to metres and grams to kilograms first. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 79.)
Choose the equation. Write it in words. You must know these equations by heart; open this bubble to hear each one. (Source: spec page 51, Appendix 7.)
Average speed equals distance moved divided by time taken. Units: metres per second. Spec statement 1.4. (Source: spec page 11, and Appendix 7 page 51.)

children.topic: Acceleration is velocity change over time
children.note: Acceleration equals change in velocity divided by time taken. a equals v minus u, all divided by t. Units: metres per second squared. Spec statement 1.6. (Source: spec page 11, and Appendix 7 page 51.)
Force equals mass times acceleration. F equals m times a. Units: newtons. Spec statement 1.17. (Source: spec page 12, and Appendix 7 page 51.)
Weight equals mass times gravitational field strength. W equals m times g. On Earth g is about 10 newtons per kilogram. Spec statement 1.18. (Source: spec page 12, and Appendix 7 page 51.)
Electrical power equals current times voltage. P equals I times V. Units: watts. Spec statement 2.4. (Source: spec page 14, and Appendix 7 page 51.)
Voltage equals current times resistance. V equals I times R. Units: volts. Spec statement 2.13. (Source: spec page 15, and Appendix 7 page 51.)
Charge equals current times time. Q equals I times t. Units: coulombs. Time must be in seconds. Spec statement 2.15. (Source: spec page 15, and Appendix 7 page 51.)
Energy transferred equals charge times voltage. E equals Q times V. Units: joules. Spec statement 2.21. (Source: spec page 15, and Appendix 7 page 51.)

children.topic: Wave speed is frequency times wavelength
children.note: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength. v equals f times lambda. Wavelength must be in metres. Spec statement 3.5. (Source: spec page 16, and Appendix 7 page 51.)
Refractive index n equals sine of the angle of incidence divided by sine of the angle of refraction. Spec statement 3.18. (Source: spec page 17, and Appendix 7 page 51.)
The sine of the critical angle c equals one divided by the refractive index n. Spec statement 3.22. (Source: spec page 18, and Appendix 7 page 51.)

Efficiency equals useful energy output divided by total energy, times one hundred percent. The spec prints total energy output; check the wording with your teacher. Spec statement 4.4. (Source: spec page 19, and Appendix 7 page 51.)

Work done equals force times distance moved in the direction of the force. W equals F times d. Work done equals energy transferred. Units: joules. Spec statement 4.11 and 4.12. (Source: spec page 20, and Appendix 7 page 51.)
Gravitational potential energy equals mass times gravitational field strength times height. Units: joules. Spec statement 4.13. (Source: spec page 20, and Appendix 7 page 51.)

children.topic: Kinetic energy: half m v squared
children.note: Kinetic energy equals one half times mass times speed squared. Units: joules. Spec statement 4.14. (Source: spec page 20, and Appendix 7 page 51.)
Density equals mass divided by volume. rho equals m divided by V. Units: kilograms per cubic metre. Spec statement 5.3. (Source: spec page 21, and Appendix 7 page 51.)
Pressure equals force divided by area. p equals F divided by A. Units: pascals. Spec statement 5.5. (Source: spec page 21, and Appendix 7 page 51.)
Pressure difference equals height times density times gravitational field strength. p equals h times rho times g. Spec statement 5.7. (Source: spec page 21, and Appendix 7 page 51.)
Write the equation, then put the numbers in, then rearrange, then work it out. Write the unit. Show every step. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 4.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Rearranging before putting the numbers in, and getting it wrong. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 4.
Not changing to standard units, like centimetres to metres or grams to kilograms. June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 55 and 80.
No working shown, so no marks for method. June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 17 and 73.
Powers of ten mistakes with standard form. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 93.
Wrong unit, or in a show that, not giving more figures than the value given. June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 75 and 99.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What do you write first in a calculation? Answer: The equation, in words or symbols. (Source: spec page 47, command words, and pages 51 to 52, equations to recall.)
Ask: Numbers first, or rearrange first? Answer: Put the numbers in first, then rearrange. (Source: spec page 47, command words, and pages 51 to 52, equations to recall.)
Ask: A length is 25 centimetres. What is it in metres? Answer: Nought point two five metres. (Source: spec page 47, command words, and pages 51 to 52, equations to recall.)
Ask: Say the equation for wave speed. Answer: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength. (Source: spec page 47, command words, and pages 51 to 52, equations to recall.)

Ask: In a show that question, how many figures do you give? Answer: At least one more significant figure than the value in the question. (Source: spec page 47, command words, and pages 51 to 52, equations to recall.)

You plot a graph, draw a diagram, or complete a table. Plot means mark the points accurately and draw a line of best fit, with a scale and labelled axes if they are not given. These are often one to three marks and test experimental skills and applying physics, assessment objectives 3 and 2. Spend about one to four minutes. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec pages 47 and 48, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 82.)
Listen for plot, draw, sketch or complete. Sketch means freehand, with labelled axes but no scale. (Source: spec page 48.)
Read the story behind the graph. A second line may need to start from the same point, not the origin. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 82.)
Check the scale on each axis. Use a sharp pencil and a ruler. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 5.)
Plot each point with a small cross. Draw one smooth line of best fit, with points spread evenly either side. Do not join the dots. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 84.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Force arrows drawn freehand, so the direction is not clear. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 5.
Joining the dots instead of drawing one line of best fit. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 84.
A plotting error, which can lose the line mark too. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 82.
Starting a second line at the origin when it should start at the same point. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 82.
Wavelength not measured between neighbouring wavefronts. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 57.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What do you draw arrows with? Answer: A ruler. (Source: spec pages 47 and 48, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 82.)
Ask: Do you join the dots on a physics graph? Answer: No. Draw one line of best fit. (Source: spec pages 47 and 48, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 82.)
Ask: What is a line of best fit? Answer: A single line with the points spread evenly on both sides. (Source: spec pages 47 and 48, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 82.)

Ask: What is the difference between sketch and plot? Answer: A sketch is freehand with no scale. A plot marks points accurately on a scale. (Source: spec pages 47 and 48, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 82.)

Ask: How do you find wavelength on a wavefront diagram? Answer: Measure the distance between two neighbouring wavefronts. (Source: spec pages 47 and 48, command words; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 82.)

These questions are about experiments: plan a method, name the variables, suggest an improvement, or evaluate data and a conclusion. They test experimental skills, assessment objective 3. About one fifth of Paper 1 marks in 2025 were for experimental skills. Spend about three to five minutes on each part. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 30, experimental skills; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 3.)
Listen for design, suggest, evaluate or comment on. Each asks for something different. (Source: spec page 47.)
Mark what is changed, what is measured, and what is kept the same. Look at the data and the graph you are given. (Source: spec page 30.)

For a method: equipment, what you change, what you measure, how, repeats, and how you get the answer. For an evaluation: look at the range, the number of points, and any odd result. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 37.)
Write numbered steps in order. When you evaluate, point to the actual data, for example one result does not fit. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 43.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Evaluating without using the data, for example saying it is not fair because of age or diet. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 37.
Adding equipment that is not needed, or not saying how the results give the answer. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 21.
Vague answers like improve accuracy or reliability. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 45.
Trivial things to keep the same, like the same ruler. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 39.
Not linking a problem, like the wire heating up, to an error or a safety risk. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 77.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What is the independent variable? Answer: The one you change. (Source: spec page 30, experimental skills; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 3.)
Ask: What is the dependent variable? Answer: The one you measure. (Source: spec page 30, experimental skills; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 3.)

Ask: Name two things to look at when you judge a graph. Answer: For example the number of points, the range, and any anomalous result. (Source: spec page 30, experimental skills; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 3.)

Ask: Is improve reliability a good answer on its own? Answer: No. Say exactly what to do, for example repeat and take a mean. (Source: spec page 30, experimental skills; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 3.)

Ask: Name one core practical in Paper 1. Answer: For example density, refraction in a glass block, or stretching a spring. (Source: spec page 30, experimental skills; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 3.)

Some questions are long answers, worth six marks. In June 2025 one asked how an electric motor works. They test knowledge and applying it, assessment objectives 1 and 2. Spend about seven or eight minutes. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 29, extended open-response questions; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 28.)
Listen for every part the question asks. The answer must cover the whole thing, not just one part. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 30.)
Mark the command word and each thing you must mention, for example the coil, the commutator and the brushes. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 28.)
Jot six short points in order, one for each mark. Use exact words, for example the current is reversed. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 61.)
Write the points as linked sentences in order: what happens first, what that causes, and the end result. A labelled diagram can help. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 34.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Explaining parts but not the whole, for example the brushes but not how the motor turns. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 30.
Saying the current changes, instead of saying it is reversed. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 28.
Mixing up the motor effect with electromagnetic induction. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 28.
Vague roles for the commutator and the brushes. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 32.
Long answers with no clear order. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 61.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: How many points do you plan for six marks? Answer: About six, one for each mark. (Source: spec page 29, extended open-response questions; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 28.)

Ask: What does the split ring commutator do? Answer: It reverses the current in the coil every half turn, so the coil keeps turning the same way. (Source: spec page 29, extended open-response questions; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 28.)

Ask: Is a motor the same as a generator? Answer: No. A motor uses a current to make a force. Induction uses movement to make a voltage. (Source: spec page 29, extended open-response questions; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 28.)
Ask: Can a diagram help? Answer: Yes, a labelled diagram as well as your writing. (Source: spec page 29, extended open-response questions; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 28.)
Ask: How long should a six mark answer take? Answer: About seven or eight minutes. That is our suggestion. (Source: spec page 29, extended open-response questions; June 2025 Paper 1 report page 28.)

nodeData.note: Edexcel International GCSE Physics, Paper 2, code 4 P H 1 slash 2 P. One hour and fifteen minutes, 70 marks, about 39 percent of the grade. You may use a calculator. Paper 2 is shorter than Paper 1, but it tests all the content, including the extra Paper 2 content shown in bold with a P in the spec. Paper 1 tests only the core. That means four more equations to learn by heart. In June 2025 the longest answer was five marks, not six. Each branch is one question type: read the question, find the key words, plan, write, check. Then five spoken questions. Draft: needs review by a physics teacher. (Source: spec pages 9 and 29.)

children.note: These questions ask you to recall a fact, a word, or a definition. Multiple choice questions also start with what, why or which. In Paper 2 they are usually worth one mark and test knowledge, assessment objective 1. Some are about the extra Paper 2 content, for example the principle of moments or evidence for the Big Bang. Spend about one minute. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 13.)
Listen for the command word. State, give and name all mean the same: recall the fact. No reason is needed. (Source: spec page 47.)
Mark the exact thing asked for, and how many. If it says choose two, choose only two. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 11.)
No plan needed. Think of the exact physics word. Time is not the same as time period. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 13.)
Write the word or the definition, short and exact. The principle of moments must be learned word for word. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 25.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in the June 2025 Paper 2. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 13.)
Writing time period, or capital T, when the answer was just time. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 13.
Choosing more options than asked. Two right and one wrong scores only one mark. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 11.
Writing only greenhouse gas, which was not enough for the mark. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 20.
Calling charges poles, or saying unlike instead of opposite charges. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 35.
Mixing up the principle of moments with conservation of momentum or energy. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 25.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: Do state, give and name mean different things? Answer: No. They all mean recall the fact. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 13.)
Ask: If a question says choose two, how many do you choose? Answer: Only two. A third wrong choice loses a mark. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 13.)

Ask: State the principle of moments. Answer: For a balanced object, the total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment about the pivot. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 13.)

Ask: Give two pieces of evidence for the Big Bang. Answer: Red-shift of galaxies, and the cosmic microwave background radiation. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 13.)
Ask: What is the period of a wave? Answer: The time for one complete wave. Its letter is capital T. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 13.)

Describe means give an account of something. Your statements should be linked, but you do not need to give a reason. In Paper 2 these are often two or three marks, for example how to use a piece of apparatus or how energy is transferred. They test knowledge, assessment objective 1. Spend about two or three minutes. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 4.)
Listen for describe. You say what happens, or what you do, in order. You do not need to say why. (Source: spec page 47.)
Mark exactly what to describe. How to use a balance is not the same as how to make results reliable. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 4.)
Count the marks. Plan one clear point for each mark. For energy, name the store it leaves, the way it is transferred, and the store it ends in. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 16.)
Write short linked sentences. Use the correct name for each piece of apparatus, for example a balance, not a scale. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 4.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in the June 2025 Paper 2. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 4.)
Writing repeat and take an average, when the question asked how to use a balance. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 4.
Taking an average instead of describing how to make one mass reading. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 5.
Being unclear which energy store is used up, for example in the Sun. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 16.
Diagrams of apparatus with missing labels or drawn carelessly. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 61.
Not using the ideas the question asks for, like forces or energy. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 61.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: Does describe need a reason? Answer: No. Say what happens. A reason is for explain. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 4.)
Ask: What do you use to measure mass? Answer: A balance. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 4.)

Ask: Light from the Sun charges a battery through a solar panel. Where does the energy end up? Answer: In the chemical store of the battery. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 4.)
Ask: How is energy carried from the Sun to the panel? Answer: By radiation. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 4.)
Ask: How many points for a three mark describe? Answer: At least three clear points. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 4.)

Explain means give a point and a reason. In Paper 2 these are often two marks, for example how a ball becomes charged, or why a further galaxy shows more red-shift. They test knowledge and applying it, assessment objectives 1 and 2. Spend about two or three minutes. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 33.)
Listen for explain. Every point needs a because. Check if you must use an earlier part of the question. (Source: spec page 47.)
Mark the facts the question gives you, for example which galaxy is further away. Use them in your answer. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 59.)
Make a chain: this happens, so that happens. For static charge, only electrons move. Positive charges never move. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 33.)
Write each link of the chain as a sentence. Say exactly what is moving or what is absorbed. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 21.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in the June 2025 Paper 2. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 33.)
Saying positive charges moved. This scores zero, whatever else you write. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 33.
Saying ions moved, instead of electrons. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 34.
Saying the rod and ball attract, but not that the charges are opposite. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 35.
Saying black is a good absorber, but not what it absorbs. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 21.
Getting the red-shift logic backwards, or not linking to earlier parts. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 59.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: A ball rubbed with a cloth becomes positive. What moved? Answer: Electrons moved off the ball. Electrons are negative. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 33.)
Ask: Do positive charges move in static electricity? Answer: No. Only electrons move. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 33.)
Ask: Why does a charged ball move towards a negative rod? Answer: The ball is positive, and opposite charges attract. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 33.)
Ask: Why does a black panel heat up faster? Answer: Black is a good absorber of infrared radiation. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 33.)
Ask: A galaxy is further away. What happens to its red-shift? Answer: It is bigger, because further galaxies move away faster. (Source: spec page 47, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 33.)

Calculate means get a number and show your working. Show that and determine questions work the same way. In Paper 2 one question can have several steps, worth up to seven marks across its parts, for example moments or a transformer. They test applying physics, assessment objective 2. On top of the Paper 1 equations, you must learn four Paper 2 equations by heart; open the Plan bubble to hear them. Spend about one minute per mark. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 47, command words, and pages 51 to 52, equations to recall.)
Read the whole question before you start. Later parts often use answers from earlier parts. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 47.)
Underline each value with its unit. Only change units if you must. Many students lost marks by changing units they did not need to. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 6.)
Choose the equation. Write it in words. You must know these by heart; open this bubble to hear the Paper 2 ones. (Source: spec page 52, Appendix 7.)
Paper 2 only. Momentum equals mass times velocity. p equals m times v. Units: kilogram metres per second. Spec statement 1.25P. (Source: spec page 12, and Appendix 7 page 52.)

Paper 2 only. Moment equals force times the perpendicular distance from the pivot. Units: newton metres. If the distance is in centimetres, the unit is newton centimetres. Spec statement 1.30P. (Source: spec page 13, and Appendix 7 page 52.)

Paper 2 only. Input voltage divided by output voltage equals primary turns divided by secondary turns. Primary means input. Secondary means output. Spec statement 6.19P. (Source: spec page 24, and Appendix 7 page 52.)

Paper 2 only. For a transformer that is one hundred percent efficient, input power equals output power. Primary voltage times primary current equals secondary voltage times secondary current. Spec statement 6.20P. (Source: spec page 24, and Appendix 7 page 52.)

Paper 2 tests all the content, so you still need every Paper 1 equation, for example wave speed, density and efficiency. Learn the four Paper 2 equations as well. (Source: spec pages 51 and 52, Appendix 7.)

Three Paper 2 equations say use, not know and use, so we think they are given in the paper: force equals change in momentum divided by time, statement 1.28P, spec page 12. Change in thermal energy equals mass times specific heat capacity times change in temperature, statement 5.13P, spec page 22. The red-shift equation, statement 8.16P, spec page 28. Check this with your teacher. (Source: spec pages 12, 22 and 28.)
Write the equation, put the numbers in, then rearrange and work it out. Label each step in words, so you still get marks if one step goes wrong. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 51.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in the June 2025 Paper 2. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 22.)
Rearranging the equation wrongly, or putting a number in the wrong place. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 22.
Changing units when it was not needed, and making a mistake. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 6.
In a show that question, not writing your value with an extra figure. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 25.
For efficiency as a percentage, forgetting to multiply by one hundred. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 48.
In red-shift, giving the change in wavelength, not the new wavelength. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 57.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: Say the equation for momentum. Answer: Momentum equals mass times velocity. (Source: spec page 47, command words, and pages 51 to 52, equations to recall.)
Ask: Say the equation for a moment. Answer: Moment equals force times perpendicular distance from the pivot. (Source: spec page 47, command words, and pages 51 to 52, equations to recall.)

Ask: A transformer has more turns on the output side. Is it step up or step down? Answer: Step up. The output voltage is bigger. (Source: spec page 47, command words, and pages 51 to 52, equations to recall.)

Ask: Should you change grams to kilograms in every density question? Answer: No. Only if you need to. Keep the units you were given and use the matching unit. (Source: spec page 47, command words, and pages 51 to 52, equations to recall.)

Ask: A galaxy moves away. Is the new wavelength longer or shorter? Answer: Longer. Add the change to the original wavelength. (Source: spec page 47, command words, and pages 51 to 52, equations to recall.)

You plot a graph, draw a trace or a diagram, or complete a table. In Paper 2 this can include drawing a new trace on an oscilloscope screen. These are often one or two marks and test experimental skills and applying physics, assessment objectives 3 and 2. Spend about one to three minutes. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec pages 47 and 48, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 14.)
Listen for plot, draw, sketch or complete. Note each change you must show, for example quieter and lower pitch. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 14.)
Quieter means a smaller amplitude. Lower pitch means a lower frequency, so a longer period. (Source: spec page 18.)
Choose the right kind of chart. Categories, like a type of material, need a bar chart, not a line graph. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 42.)
Draw with a pencil and a ruler, then label every part. Do not use an erasable pen; rubbed out lines still show on the scan. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 14.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in the June 2025 Paper 2. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 14.)
Drawing a trace with the same or a shorter period, not longer. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 14.
Using an erasable pen, so rubbed out lines still show up. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 14.
Thinking a bar chart and a line graph are interchangeable. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 42.
Apparatus diagrams not labelled, or not drawn accurately. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 61.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: A sound gets quieter. What happens to the trace? Answer: The amplitude gets smaller. The waves are less tall. (Source: spec pages 47 and 48, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 14.)

Ask: A sound gets lower in pitch. What happens to the trace? Answer: The period gets longer. The waves are more spread out. (Source: spec pages 47 and 48, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 14.)
Ask: Which chart for a categoric variable, like a type of material? Answer: A bar chart. (Source: spec pages 47 and 48, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 14.)
Ask: What do you draw a graph line with? Answer: A sharp pencil. Use a ruler for straight lines. (Source: spec pages 47 and 48, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 14.)
Ask: Why avoid erasable pen? Answer: Rubbed out work can still show up on the scanned paper. (Source: spec pages 47 and 48, command words; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 14.)

These questions are about experiments: name the variables, say what to keep the same, suggest an improvement, or use data to test a claim. In Paper 2 they include the extra practicals, for example charging by friction and the speed of sound. They test experimental skills, assessment objective 3. Spend about two to four minutes on each part. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 30, experimental skills; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 46.)
Listen for suggest, comment on, or evaluate. Check what the experiment is really measuring. (Source: spec page 47.)
Mark what is changed, what is measured, and which way things move. The direction of a result matters. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 43.)
To test a claim from a graph, pick two points and work out the same quantity for both. Then compare them. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 46.)
Quote the numbers you worked out, then give your conclusion and the reason for it. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 46.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in the June 2025 Paper 2. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 45.)
Vague answers like improve accuracy or reliability. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 45.
Trivial things to keep the same, like the same ruler or string. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 39.
Changing something that changes the whole experiment, like the ball. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 40.
A conclusion with no data and no calculation scored zero. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 46.
Ignoring which way the ball moved, so the analysis was wrong. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 44.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What is a control variable? Answer: Something you keep the same so the test is fair. (Source: spec page 30, experimental skills; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 46.)
Ask: Is the same ruler a good control variable? Answer: No. It is too trivial. Choose something that affects the result. (Source: spec page 30, experimental skills; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 46.)

Ask: How do you test if two quantities are inversely proportional? Answer: Multiply them together at two or more points. If the answer stays the same, they are inversely proportional. (Source: spec page 30, experimental skills; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 46.)

Ask: Name one extra Paper 2 practical. Answer: For example charging by friction, the speed of sound, or specific heat capacity. (Source: spec page 30, experimental skills; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 46.)
Ask: Is improve reliability a good answer on its own? Answer: No. Say exactly what to do. (Source: spec page 30, experimental skills; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 46.)

Some questions need a longer, linked answer. In the June 2025 Paper 2 the longest was five marks, about using transformers in the national grid. There was also a three mark answer about energy transfers. They test knowledge and applying it, assessment objectives 1 and 2. Spend about five or six minutes on a five mark answer. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's. (Source: spec page 29, extended open-response questions; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 53.)
Count the marks and note every part the question asks for. Use the marks as a guide to how much to write. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 61.)
Mark the main words, for example step-up, step-down, transmission and safety. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 53.)
Jot one point for each mark, in order: where the transformer goes, what it does to voltage and current, and why. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 55.)
Write the points as linked sentences in order. A clear labelled diagram can earn marks too. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 55.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in the June 2025 Paper 2. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 53.)
Not saying why: less energy wasted as heat, or lower voltage for safety. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 53.
Confusing which energy store is used up in the Sun. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 16.
Mixing two different ways of describing energy in one answer. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 16.
Weaker answers struggled to build a logical description. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 3.
Long answers with no clear order or sequence. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 61.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.

Ask: Where is the step-up transformer in the national grid? Answer: Between the power station and the transmission cables. (Source: spec page 29, extended open-response questions; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 53.)
Ask: What does a step-up transformer do to the current? Answer: It makes the current smaller. (Source: spec page 29, extended open-response questions; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 53.)
Ask: Why is a smaller current better in the cables? Answer: Less energy is wasted by heating the cables. (Source: spec page 29, extended open-response questions; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 53.)
Ask: Why is a step-down transformer used near homes? Answer: To lower the voltage so it is safer to use. (Source: spec page 29, extended open-response questions; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 53.)
Ask: How many points do you plan for five marks? Answer: About five, one for each mark. (Source: spec page 29, extended open-response questions; June 2025 Paper 2 report page 53.)
